blocks.content: Look around the room you are sitting in right now. A chair, a phone, a cup of coffee, even you, the reader. Every single one of these things has properties (a phone has a color, a brand, a battery percentage) and behavior (a phone can ring, vibrate, take a photo).

The moment you start writing software that needs to represent real things like this, cars, users, bank accounts, game characters, you run into a question: how do you turn a real-world "thing" into code? That exact question is what Classes and Objects answer, and it is the single most foundational idea in all of object-oriented design.
1. Introduction & Why It Matters

A class is a template or blueprint that describes what a group of similar things looks like and what they can do. An object is one real, concrete thing built from that template. Think of it this way: "Car" is a class (a general idea: every car has a brand, a model, fuel), while "my neighbor's red Honda Civic" is an object (one specific, real car sitting in a driveway).

Imagine writing a video game with 200 enemy characters, and you had no concept of a "class." You would have to write 200 separate blocks of code, each redeclaring health, position, attack power, and the exact same movement logic, one variable and one function at a time. Without classes, there is no reusable structure, bugs would multiply because fixing "how an enemy takes damage" would mean fixing it in 200 different places instead of one. Classes solve this by letting you define the shape and behavior once, and then stamp out as many objects from it as you need.
2. Real-Life Analogy
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847616896-591064582.png
blocks.alt: Real world entities like Car, Dog and Person abstracted into a single reusable Class concept

blocks.content: Picture three completely different real-world things: a car, a dog, and a person. They seem unrelated, but each one has a name, a set of properties, and a set of things it can "do." Your brain automatically groups "things that share a shape" into a category, that mental grouping is exactly what a class does in code.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847618836-677267901.png
blocks.alt: One blueprint used to construct three separate houses

blocks.content: The classic analogy, and it is classic because it is genuinely the best one, is a construction blueprint. An architect draws ONE blueprint for a house design, that blueprint is not a house you can live in, it is just a plan on paper. A construction company can use that same blueprint to build House 1, House 2, and House 3. All three houses share the same layout, but each is a physically separate building, you can paint House 1 blue without affecting the others. The blueprint is the class. Each house is an object.
3. Problem It Solves & Definition

Classes solve the problem of modeling real-world entities in a reusable, maintainable way. Before object-oriented programming, developers used procedural code, plain functions operating on loose, disconnected data, which made large systems hard to reason about as they grew. Classes bundle data (state) and the functions that operate on that data (behavior) into one unit, called encapsulation.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.content: A class is a user-defined data type that groups related fields (state) and methods (behavior) into a single reusable unit, serving as the template from which individual objects are instantiated at runtime. In simple terms: a class is a blueprint for creating objects, and an object is a specific instance created from that blueprint, with its own copy of the data described by the class.
4. Key Terminology

["Class: the blueprint or template that defines fields and methods.","Object: a concrete instance created from a class, living in memory.","Instance: another word for object, \"instance of a class\" and \"object of a class\" mean the same thing.","Field (also called attribute or member variable): a piece of data that belongs to every object of the class, e.g. brand, fuelLevel.","Method: a function defined inside a class that describes behavior, e.g. drive(), refuel().","Constructor: a special method that runs exactly once, at the moment an object is created with the new keyword, to set up its initial state.","this keyword: inside a method or constructor, this refers to the specific object the method was called on.","Instantiation: the act of creating an object from a class, done with the new keyword.","Reference variable: a variable that holds the memory address pointing to where the object lives, not the object itself."]
items: Class: the blueprint or template that defines fields and methods.
Object: a concrete instance created from a class, living in memory.
Instance: another word for object, "instance of a class" and "object of a class" mean the same thing.
Field (also called attribute or member variable): a piece of data that belongs to every object of the class, e.g. brand, fuelLevel.
Method: a function defined inside a class that describes behavior, e.g. drive(), refuel().
Constructor: a special method that runs exactly once, at the moment an object is created with the new keyword, to set up its initial state.
this keyword: inside a method or constructor, this refers to the specific object the method was called on.
Instantiation: the act of creating an object from a class, done with the new keyword.
Reference variable: a variable that holds the memory address pointing to where the object lives, not the object itself.

blocks.content: 5. Visual Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847620709-196119193.png
blocks.alt: Anatomy of a Car class showing fields, constructor and methods as three parts of one blueprint

blocks.content: Every class you will ever write, no matter how complex, is really made of the same three ingredients shown above: fields that hold state, a constructor that sets up a new object’s starting state, and methods that define what the object can do. Once you can spot these three parts, reading any unfamiliar class becomes much easier.
6. Syntax & Code Example
A Java class always follows the same skeleton, a constructor always shares the exact name of the class and has no return type, not even void:

["class is the keyword that starts a class definition, by convention ClassName starts with a capital letter.","fields declare the state, no value assigned yet, just the shape.","this.fieldName explicitly refers to the object’s own field, disambiguating it from a same-named constructor parameter."]
items: class is the keyword that starts a class definition, by convention ClassName starts with a capital letter.
fields declare the state, no value assigned yet, just the shape.
this.fieldName explicitly refers to the object’s own field, disambiguating it from a same-named constructor parameter.

blocks.content: Let us write one small, complete, runnable example: a Car class, plus a Main class that actually creates and uses two Car objects.

codes.python:
# The Car class: the blueprint every Car object below is built from
class Car:

    def __init__(self, brand, model):
        # Fields: the STATE every Car object carries around
        self.brand = brand
        self.model = model
        self.fuel_level = 100  # every new car starts with a full tank

    def drive(self, distance_km):
        # BEHAVIOR - driving consumes fuel
        fuel_used = distance_km // 10  # simple rule: 10km costs 1% fuel
        self.fuel_level = max(0, self.fuel_level - fuel_used)  # never let fuel go negative
        print(f"{self.brand} {self.model} drove {distance_km}km. Fuel left: {self.fuel_level}%")

    def refuel(self):
        # BEHAVIOR - refueling resets the tank
        self.fuel_level = 100
        print(f"{self.brand} {self.model} refueled to 100%")

    def get_fuel_level(self):
        # exposes the fuel_level field in a controlled, read-only way
        return self.fuel_level


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Two separate objects, built from the SAME Car class
    car1 = Car("Honda", "Civic")
    car2 = Car("Tesla", "Model 3")

    car1.drive(250)
    car2.drive(80)

    car1.refuel()

    print("car1 fuel:", car1.get_fuel_level())
    print("car2 fuel:", car2.get_fuel_level())

blocks.content: Here is exactly what happens to each object at every step:

{"headers":["Step","Statement","car1 state","car2 state"],"rows":[["1","car1 = new Car(\"Honda\",\"Civic\")","brand=Honda, model=Civic, fuel=100","does not exist yet"],["2","car2 = new Car(\"Tesla\",\"Model 3\")","fuel=100","brand=Tesla, model=Model 3, fuel=100"],["3","car1.drive(250)","fuelUsed=25, fuel=100 minus 25=75","fuel=100"],["4","car2.drive(80)","fuel=75","fuelUsed=8, fuel=100 minus 8=92"],["5","car1.refuel()","fuel resets to 100","fuel=92"],["6","print both fuel levels","prints 100","prints 92"]]}
Now let’s see exactly where all of this actually lives in memory:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847622544-382098316.png
blocks.alt: Stack holding references, Heap holding the actual objects, Method Area holding shared class metadata, String Pool holding shared literals

blocks.content: 8.1 Stack, Heap and Method Area

The local variables car1 and car2 are pushed onto the stack, but they only hold a reference pointing to where the real object lives. The two actual Car objects, with their real field values, are created on the heap, this is why they are independent, each new Car() call carves out a fresh block of heap memory.
8.2 Shared Class Metadata

The Car class itself, its method bytecode and structural metadata, is loaded into the method area exactly once, no matter how many Car objects you create. Both car1 and car2 share this one copy; only their field data is duplicated on the heap. String literals like "Honda" are stored in a special part of the heap called the string pool, and reused if the same literal appears again.
9. Behind the Scenes (JVM Internals)
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784847624152-111858405.png
blocks.alt: Compilation and class loading pipeline from source file to a live object on the heap

blocks.content: The javac compiler turns your human-readable Car.java into Car.class, a file of JVM bytecode, this happens once, before the program ever runs. The first time your running program actually needs the Car class, the JVM’s ClassLoader reads Car.class and stores its structure in the method area, this loading step happens only once per class, ever. Every subsequent new Car(...) call skips the loading step and goes straight to allocating a fresh block on the heap, running the constructor, and handing back a reference to it.

blocks.alt: A plain class scanned by the Spring container and turned into a managed bean object

blocks.content: In Spring Boot, you write a plain class and Spring’s container scans it, then creates and manages the actual object (called a "bean") on your behalf. In Hibernate, an @Entity-annotated class like Car maps directly to a database table, where each row corresponds to one Car object. The Java Collections framework is built the same way: an ArrayList is a class, and every list you create is a separate object of that one class.
11. Advantages & Limitations

{"headers":["Advantages","Limitations"],"rows":[["Reusability: write the Car class once, create as many Car objects as needed without duplicating logic.","Overhead for trivial data: wrapping a single number in a full class can be unnecessary ceremony."],["Encapsulation: private fields protect each object’s state from being changed carelessly from outside code.","Overuse leads to God Classes: cramming too many unrelated fields and methods into one class makes it hard to change safely."],["Maintainability: fixing a bug in drive() fixes it for every current and future Car object.","Not always the right tool: some problems are better expressed with simple functions than a full class hierarchy."]]}
12. Common Mistakes & Best Practices
12.1 Common Mistakes

["Making every field public \"just to make it easier,\" which throws away encapsulation and lets outside code corrupt an object’s state.","Forgetting that this.fieldName and the constructor parameter are different things when they share a name, leading to fields silently never getting set.","Assuming two objects created from the same class somehow share their field values, they do not, each has its own independent copy on the heap.","Cramming unrelated responsibilities into a single class instead of splitting them into focused classes."]
items: Making every field public "just to make it easier," which throws away encapsulation and lets outside code corrupt an object’s state.
Forgetting that this.fieldName and the constructor parameter are different things when they share a name, leading to fields silently never getting set.
Assuming two objects created from the same class somehow share their field values, they do not, each has its own independent copy on the heap.
Cramming unrelated responsibilities into a single class instead of splitting them into focused classes.

blocks.content: 12.2 Best Practices

["Keep fields private and expose controlled access through methods, ideally behavior methods like drive() instead of raw setters.","Give a class exactly one clear responsibility (the Single Responsibility Principle), a Car class should describe a car, not also handle payment.","Always validate incoming data inside the constructor when it matters, so an object can never exist in an invalid state.","Name classes as nouns (Car, Account) and methods as verbs (drive, refuel), this alone makes code dramatically more readable."]
items: Keep fields private and expose controlled access through methods, ideally behavior methods like drive() instead of raw setters.
Give a class exactly one clear responsibility (the Single Responsibility Principle), a Car class should describe a car, not also handle payment.
Always validate incoming data inside the constructor when it matters, so an object can never exist in an invalid state.
Name classes as nouns (Car, Account) and methods as verbs (drive, refuel), this alone makes code dramatically more readable.

blocks.content: 13. Key Takeaways & Cheat Sheet

["A class is a reusable blueprint; an object is one concrete instance built from that blueprint.","Fields hold state, methods define behavior, and the constructor sets up a new object’s starting state.","Every object gets its own independent copy of the fields on the heap, while the class definition is loaded into the method area only once and shared by all objects.","this refers to the current object, letting you tell a field apart from a same-named parameter.","Encapsulation, keeping fields private and controlling access through methods, is what makes classes safe to build large systems on top of."]

Fields hold state, methods define behavior, and the constructor sets up a new object’s starting state.
Every object gets its own independent copy of the fields on the heap, while the class definition is loaded into the method area only once and shared by all objects.
this refers to the current object, letting you tell a field apart from a same-named parameter.
Encapsulation, keeping fields private and controlling access through methods, is what makes classes safe to build large systems on top of.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: If asked "what is a class vs an object," the fastest correct answer is: a class is the blueprint, an object is one instance built from it, each object has its own state but shares the same behavior defined in the class.
